Historical observations for this pairing come from a mix of tide gauges and satellites. Tide gauges are devices that measure sea level relative to the shoreline. Many coastal cities have had working tide gauges for a half-century or more. Satellite instruments can measure changes in the height of the ocean surface around the world. The long-term reconstruction back to 1880 comes from tide gauges but has been adjusted to represent a global average.

Projections are scenarios that were updated in 2022 by a U.S. federal task force to incorporate the best available scientific knowledge on sea level rise. The trajectories are based on a variety of observed and modeled studies and were used in the most recent National Climate Assessment. Future projections generally look smoother than the historical trends, in part because they are graphed at 10-year intervals.

This feature distinguishes between two types of sea level rise. Global sea level rise refers to the average height of the ocean surface worldwide, relative to the center of the Earth. Local or relative sea level rise is measured in relation to the shoreline, which itself can rise or fall as described above. Local sea level rise is especially important when considering impacts on coastal land and infrastructure.

How much sea levels will rise, especially beyond 2100, depends heavily on how quickly ice will melt from Antarctica and Greenland.[3] While scientists are improving models to better understand these risks, because these processes are still uncertain, it is hard to predict exactly how high seas will rise. However, even small changes in sea level can have profound effects on coastal communities.
